claims.text: An occupation is a person's regular type of work or job, and an individual's choice of occupation is the decision about which type of work to take up, made by weighing the wage on offer against non-wage factors.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The factors affecting an individual's choice of occupation include the wage on offer and non-wage factors: the skills and qualifications the person already holds, the training a job provides, working conditions and hours, security of employment, distance from home and family, personal interest and aptitude, and the status the job carries.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Because priorities differ between individuals, one worker may take an occupation that pays less where its non-wage package - hours, security, training or location - fits that worker's situation, whereas another worker facing the same offers may take the higher wage.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Workers are classified into the primary, secondary or tertiary sector through the industry that employs them, because the labels classify industries by what they do - taking materials from nature, making things, or providing services - so "primary" names a sector of industry, not a type or rank of worker.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Wage determination is the process by which the wage paid for a job is set: employers demand workers, workers supply their time and skill, and the wage settles at the level where the number of workers employers seek matches the number offering to work.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where employers seek more workers than are available at the going wage, they tend to bid the wage up to attract and keep staff, and where more workers offer themselves than employers seek, the wage tends to be bid down or held flat.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Wages differ between occupations and between places because the demand for workers and the supply of available workers differ in each local labour market.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A rise in demand for a firm's product tends to raise the firm's demand for workers, and employers competing for a limited number of trained workers tend to offer a higher wage to fill the posts, because each vacancy left unfilled costs them output.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Earnings differ between occupations because of differences in the skill and qualifications demanded, the scarcity of the workers who hold them, the length and cost of training, experience and responsibility, the risk and conditions of the work, and the balance of demand and supply in each occupation.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Workers whose skills are scarce and take years to acquire tend to earn more, because employers must compete against each other for the small number of qualified people, whereas workers whose skills are common face weaker competition for their services and lower pay.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A labour-market diagram is described with the wage on the vertical axis and the number of workers on the horizontal axis; a rise in demand for an occupation shifts its demand curve outward, and the new balance shows a higher wage with more workers employed.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where high earnings in an occupation attract many new trainees over time, the supply of qualified workers grows and the earnings premium of that occupation tends to narrow, provided employers' demand does not keep growing faster.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The division of labour, also called specialisation, is the splitting of production into separate narrow tasks so that each worker concentrates on one task instead of making the whole product, and output per worker tends to rise as a result.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Specialisation tends to raise output per worker because practice at one narrow task builds speed and skill, no time is lost moving between tasks, and training a new worker for one task takes less time than teaching the whole craft.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The drawbacks of specialisation fall on different parties: for the worker, repeating one narrow task may bring boredom and ties the worker's livelihood to a single task, while drawbacks at the level of the whole economy, such as depending on a narrow range of production, are a separate matter from the worker's own position.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Examination answers about the division of labour must match the party the question names: benefits or drawbacks for the worker, for the employing firm and for the whole economy are distinct, and the test is to ask whose position the answer changes.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Relative bargaining power affects the wage: where workers bargain collectively through a trade union, or hold skills an employer finds hard to replace, they tend to secure a higher wage than workers bargaining one by one, whereas where one or a few large employers face many job-seekers, the employers' stronger position tends to hold the wage down.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A minimum wage is the lowest wage, usually stated per hour, that an employer may legally pay a worker; it is one way government policy influences wages, alongside the pay scales the government sets as an employer and laws requiring equal pay for work of equal value.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A minimum wage set above the market wage raises the pay of low-paid workers who keep their jobs, but at the higher wage employers demand fewer workers while more people seek work, so an excess supply of labour opens up and unemployment among the low-paid may rise; the more elastic the demand for that labour, the larger the fall in employment. A minimum wage set below the market wage leaves the wage paid unchanged.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

notes: Corrected 2026-10-13: elasticity of labour demand sets the size of the job loss from a binding minimum wage, not whether there is one (plan fix, CM-0455-MINWAGE-UNEMPLOYMENT).

claims.text: Discrimination in the labour market is treating workers differently in pay, hiring, training or promotion for reasons unrelated to their productivity, such as gender, race or age; it tends to lower the earnings of the group discriminated against, through lower pay for the same work and through exclusion from better-paid posts.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Bargaining strength and government policy both shift earnings between groups of workers: workers in a strong trade union tend to earn more than similar non-union workers, a minimum wage set above the market wage lifts the lowest earnings, equal-pay laws aim to remove pay gaps that rest on discrimination, and the government's own pay scales set earnings across the public sector.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Earnings differ between the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors through the skill, productivity and balance of demand and supply in each industry rather than through the sector label: farm labour in the primary sector tends to be low-paid because many unskilled workers compete for the work and output per worker is low, while skilled mine workers in the same sector tend to earn several times as much, and the tertiary sector ranges from low-paid shop work to highly paid banking.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: On average women tend to earn less than men, because more women work in lower-paid occupations and part-time, career breaks to care for children reduce experience and promotion, and some employers discriminate; equal-pay laws and a minimum wage aim to narrow the gap.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Public-sector pay is set mainly through government pay scales limited by the government's budget and tends to come with greater job security and a pension, while private-sector pay follows each firm's demand for labour and its profits; as a result highly skilled professionals tend to earn more in the private sector, while lower-skilled workers may earn more in the public sector.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A rise in the supply of workers to an occupation is shown on a labour-market diagram by the supply curve shifting to the right; at the old wage more workers offer themselves than employers seek, so, with demand unchanged, the wage falls to a new equilibrium at which more workers are employed.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: For the firm, the division of labour tends to raise output per worker and lower the average cost of each unit, but where one stage halts the whole line may stop, and repetitive work may raise absence, staff turnover and mistakes, which add to the firm's costs.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: For the economy, specialisation tends to raise total output and lets regions and countries trade what they produce best, but it may leave a region dependent on a narrow range of products, and workers whose specialised skills do not transfer may face long spells of unemployment when demand for that product falls.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
